title: Can you realistically do game development on a $20 Claude Code?
author: arangar
selftext:
Been using some Claude at Work, and doing basic python coding it feels like I burn through $20 very quick (on Sonnet) - Can you realistically expect to do game dev on a $20 plan?

  
(I use a simple multi role setup where I align with one Agent on architecture to create tight briefs for a devloper Agent)

comments.author: MeasuredCuriosity

replies.author: ArchitectNebulous
replies.body: How would you optimize the project files and context for larger projects?  Context scope has been the biggest killer on my $20plan.

replies.author: MeasuredCuriosity
replies.body:
In my experience it gets significantly harder, but there are things that can help:  
1. Make it easier to get context:  I've used this tool: [https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify) It's hard to quantify exactly how much it helps but I think it does make it faster and cheaper to regain context

2. Minimize the context needed: Keep your modules/components clean and separated from each other. You may need the context for the interface, but not the implementation. Keeping strong defined boundaries can help.

I'm sure others may have lots of tips to maximize efficiency, all of which can help, but with a bigger project things will scale up fast. Just like it's harder for a single person to keep track of a large project, AI tools will also struggle.

replies.author: TheRealLunicuss
replies.body: There are so, so many ways. Minimising context usage is quite an enormous topic. You could do something simple like disable artifacts to clear about 10k tokens from the system prompt. You could try and make your codebase less coupled so that the AI can get away with loading fewer files to get anything done. You could make sure Claude's memory isn't flooded with useless information. Setup rules so that Claude only loads local context and maintains the same signatures when asked to fix simple bugs. If you have a "work is finished" flow described in [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md), move it to a skill that only loads when the work is actually finished. Etc etc. There are endless possibilities, you keep it in your mind and you'll spot optimisations.

comments.author: Kingfish344
comments.body: I am using Claude and codex both at $20. Originally had just been using claude but now that I added Codex I like them auditing each other. I use mostly sonnet with opus occasionally and have run out of tokens on both, but 5 hour refresh is generally alright. I will say codex is more efficient on token use. My view is be aware of what eats up the tokens will make your life better. Create new sessions for differing activities. Compact all the time. Add key things to memory and remove the noise from memory. All these make it quite viable, just got to be diligent. Also, notice token burn is way higher during high usage times than lower usage times. So, 1 pm on a Monday is going to get you.

comments.author: CycleMother2006

Your 20$ will take you farther with Codex.

And yes, especially if you want to do it well. Because if you want to do your game well, you'll be spending a lot of time learning game design fundamentals and working on aesthetics and various avenues where your tokens aren't going to help you as much, which means you aren't constantly prompting and chugging through them. If you're willing to work with AI rather than just have it do everything and handhold for you, you can make your tokens go 3-4x as long too since you won't have to tell it to do stupid simple tasks like, "Shift this house 40 pixels over." and can just take 2 seconds to make the adjustment yourself. You wouldn't believe how many tokens people burn on requests they could handle faster than the time it took to make the request.
